entries.title: Check out our free livestream during National Veterans Small Business Week.
entries.summary: Join our November 2026 YouTube livestream for National Veterans Small Business Week. Master AI skills with Gemini and get 1:1 coaching. Register today.
entries.content:
In honor of National Veterans Small Business Week, Grow with Google, American Corporate Partners (ACP), and Blue Star Families are hosting the third annual National Veterans Small Business Week livestream on Monday, November 9 at 1:00 p.m. Eastern.

Across the country, 1.6 million veteran entrepreneurs employ over 3.3 million workers and grow local economies. This free YouTube livestream shares practical AI skills for veteran and mil-spouse entrepreneurs to streamline their operations, reach customers, and grow their businesses.

Highlights include:

  • Hands-on training: Learn how to use AI to run and grow your business
  • Veteran entrepreneur spotlight: Hear from Adam Baker, founder and CEO of veteran-owned pet toy company SodaPup about his journey.
  • Live Q&A: Ask questions and learn about resources from ACP and Blue Star Families.
  • Exclusive post-event coaching: Sign up for a complimentary 30-minute 1:1 virtual coaching session with a Grow with Google Coach.

Register today at goo.gle/NVSBW26.

entries.title: Watch Henry Cavill build a video game on his Googlebook
entries.summary: The video shows the making of Henry Cavill's game, “Mustache Protocol."
entries.content:
Actor, producer, and tech enthusiast Henry Cavill has been putting Googlebook to the ultimate test, and one thing’s become clear: going from an idea to action is effortless on this laptop. Naturally, Henry wanted to push Googlebook’s limits. But could he take a back-of-the-napkin game concept and build a fully playable 16-bit video game on his Googlebook?

With built-in AI tools like Antigravity, which can translate natural language prompts into working 16-bit game mechanics, and Rambler, a speech-to-text tool that polishes raw thoughts, Henry set off to bring his retro arcade dream to life — with a little help from Google.

Check out “Mustache Protocol”

Every video game needs a hook, and Henry’s was inspired by his internet-famous mustache lore. The game, “Mustache Protocol,” is about stopping rogue CGI artists from erasing every mustache on the planet.

While refining the game, Henry used Rambler on his Googlebook to organize his thoughts as he brainstormed. He mocked up different aesthetics, added accessories, and fine-tuned the design with Magic Pointer, which let him select and combine visual elements on screen. Plus, with Continue On, Henry was able to move from his Android phone to his Googlebook and back without losing context or interrupting his creative flow.

Watch the series and play to support Movember

Today, we’re launching a new series that shows what went into bringing the game to life. The episodes will detail how Henry designed the hero character, vibe coded meme-inspired superpowers, and added to the game’s soundtrack. We’ll drop new episodes in the weeks ahead — and when the game is finished, you will be able to play it to support men's health.

We’re teaming up with Movember to donate $11 for every play during the month of November, up to $500,000. Funding will help support awareness and funding for men's mental health, suicide prevention, prostate cancer, and testicular cancer.

Dive into the first episode today. Visit googlebook.com/henry to watch more episodes and sign up for game launch updates.

entries.title: We're sharing our framework for building safer and more helpful AI for health.
entries.summary: Many of us have turned to AI with a health question or received care from a doctor who’s using it. The adoption of technology for health is accelerating and impacts bill…
entries.content:
Many of us have turned to AI with a health question or received care from a doctor who’s using it. The adoption of technology for health is accelerating and impacts billions of people every day. But how can we assess if these tools are safe and helpful?

In partnership with health experts Dr. Elizabeth McGlynn and Dr. Dana Gelb Safran, we published a whitepaper detailing an end-to-end evaluation approach to assess AI use cases for addressing people’s health needs. The framework evaluates models across three areas: accuracy, safety, and usefulness. It combines closed-question benchmarks, autoraters, and expert human review to assess common and high-risk health scenarios.

We built and continue to utilize this framework to assess whether our models provide useful, accurate responses that promote safe interactions in health contexts. By sharing our methodology, we hope to promote transparency in how we approach this important area, and seek to support the entire health ecosystem — from developers to researchers to clinicians — in building AI tools people can trust.

entries.title: Take a closer look at art with the Courtauld
entries.summary: Experts from the Courtauld discuss their digital partnership with Google Arts & Culture, demonstrating how ultra-high-resolution imagery brings gallery masterpieces into focus. Focusing on works like Paul Cézanne's still life, they explore hidden brushstr
entries.content:
Today, we are delighted to launch ‘The Art of Looking’, a major expansion of the partnership between Google Arts & Culture and the Courtauld Institute of Art. This collection, which brings together art made across centuries and continents, reflects a shared commitment to opening up art and art history to the broadest possible audience, in keeping with the Courtauld’s commitment to art for all. Additionally, we’re jointly announcing a new artist residency to explore how AI can be used for metadata workflows in cultural institutions.

The 12 new stories in ‘The Art of Looking’ take on some of the most fundamental questions we can ask about art. In ‘What does art mean?’ Professor Dorothy Price shows how the painter Lubaina Himid used her imagination to rewrite history, while in ‘Who is art for?’ Dr. Tom Stammers traces how artist Rosa Bonheur bypassed the elite gatekeepers of her day to reach a global audience. The stories also take us closer to how artists made the works themselves: zoom into the bold marks of Van Gogh’s reed pens, explore the enduring riddle of Michelangelo’s The Dream, or discover with Dr. Jessica Barker how Claudette Johnson uses the monumental scale of Blues Dance to give her subjects a powerful presence.

Founded in 1932 as the first institution in the UK devoted to the study of art history, the Courtauld is today an internationally renowned center for teaching and research, as well as a major public gallery. It is home to the largest community of art historians and conservators in the UK, and its scholars have long been pioneers in using technology, from X-rays to chemistry, to reveal what lies beneath the surface of works of art. Making its collection — and the research behind it — accessible to audiences across the globe remains a central priority.

Google Arts & Culture first partnered with The Courtauld in 2022, using Google’s Art Camera to capture 16 iconic works in remarkable depth and detail. For the first time, anyone, anywhere could follow the extraordinary play of Manet’s brushstrokes across the surface of “A Bar at the Folies-Bergère”.

Artist residency

In addition to The Art of Looking, the Courtauld and Google Arts & Culture are announcing a new artist residency to explore how AI can unlock the Courtauld’s extensive photographic collections. It lays the foundation for making these images searchable and connecting them to learning curricula worldwide.

We look forward to seeing how these tools can open up art education to new audiences and create even more immersive ways of learning. Explore The Art of Looking today at goo.gle/courtauld.

entries.title: Designing responsible AI for learning
entries.summary: A teacher pointing at a student's Chromebook screen while the student observes.
entries.content:
If you’ve ever watched a student use AI tools to help with their schoolwork, you’ve probably wondered: Are they actually learning, or just finding a shortcut? Questions like this are important, and they guide our work when building products for learning.

We believe technology paired with great educators can unlock incredible learning potential, and we’re focused on building technology responsibly to help students thrive. Today, we’re making important updates to our products used in schools, including building Guided Learning capabilities into Google Search and Google Classroom, and evolving our approach to school controls.

Developing products built for learning

We believe AI products should support “productive struggle” — enabling students to be actively challenged without getting so overwhelmed that they give up. That’s the philosophy behind Guided Learning. In Gemini, Guided Learning acts as an interactive study tool that coaches students through the process of problem solving through open-ended questions and step-by-step breakdowns. Our research shows that Guided Learning leads to measurable learning gains for students, and we’re now bringing Guided Learning to more products.

  • Google Search: We’re building Guided Learning capabilities into Search for student accounts to help them work through problems without skipping straight to answers. When our systems understand a student is looking for certain types of homework help, Search will walk them through the topic or problem step by step. For example, if a student pastes a complex physics problem or asks for help writing a book report in Search, they’ll see prompts to help them think critically and work through the concepts, without going directly to the answer. We’re starting with a pilot in select U.S. schools later this month to gather and incorporate educator feedback before expanding to other school districts in the coming months.

Google Classroom: Starting today, Guided Learning is globally available in Google Classroom, a central hub where teachers and students organize schoolwork, share assignments and stay connected. When a student starts a Guided Learning activity assigned by their teacher, it acts like a 1-1 study tool, anchored in class material to help them stay on task. It also gives teachers real-time insights to spot where the class might need extra support.

Before launching Guided Learning in Google Classroom, we worked closely with schools and educators to test the feature and integrate their feedback.

Enhancing school controls

We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach. After listening to schools, teachers, leading researchers, and policymakers, we are now updating our approach to controls for Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search. Access to these products will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on.

We’ll share more specifics with schools in the coming months ahead of the changes rolling out so they have time to prepare and enable a smooth transition. Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit.

We’ll continue to listen to feedback and evolve our approach as we work in partnership with schools, teachers, pedagogical experts, and parents on helping the next generation learn and thrive.

entries.title: AI in the learning era
entries.summary: Read announcements from Google’s 2026 AI in the Learning Era event.
entries.content:
We’re announcing major updates to our education portfolio: launching Guided Learning into Google Classroom globally, bringing Guided Learning capabilities to Google Search, and updating our approach to controls for Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search for K-12 student accounts. We’re also sharing new research, new Google.org funding, and expanding AI training for educators.

Read our full collection of updates below to learn how we’re building technology purpose-built for education. And check out more on our approach in our AI in Education report.

entries.title: We’re providing funding for organizations building AI for teachers.
entries.summary: Google.org is funding five organizations to build AI tools for teachers. See how these initiatives support educators and students. Get the details.
entries.content:
Google.org has long supported teachers and students, including free AI training for educators. Today, Google.org is providing over $9.5 million in funding across five organizations building with and for educators, aiming to help millions of students reach their full potential:

  • The City University of New York: Helping educators build digital and computational literacy through the Computing Integrated Teacher Education (CITE) initiative
  • Fab AI: Collaborating with Google DeepMind and the Gates Foundation to build open models that help teachers plan lessons and support early reading
  • Krause Center for Innovation: Helping school districts bring responsible AI education into classrooms
  • Teaching Lab: Piloting Coherence OS, an operating system that gives teachers and leaders real-time support
  • 1EdTech Global: Building public infrastructure for trusted learning standards

entries.title: Working collaboratively to fight scams in Asia Pacific
entries.summary: A woman using her smartphone, surrounded by graphic icons representing online security, privacy, and message alerts.
entries.content:
Scams are growing more complex, fueled by increasingly sophisticated tactics from transnational crime groups. A recent UN report illustrated the effect these scams have across the Asia Pacific (APAC) region. In 2025, scam losses across East Asia, Southeast Asia, Australia, and New Zealand reached up to $114.1 billion USD, with over 40% of ASEAN consumers said to be experiencing scams.

Tackling these highly organized networks requires a unified effort. Today, we are sharing how, at Google, we are scaling our defenses to protect APAC communities. This includes built-in protections across products and platforms, industry-wide collaboration, and new local partnerships to increase community resilience.

Built-in protections across devices and platforms

Our first line of defense is to secure the devices and platforms people use every day. This year, Android launched Fake Call Detection, a feature designed to spot AI-driven phone call impersonation. Built on open RCS technology, other platforms can adopt the same protections. On Pixel, built-in scam detection now alerts you to potential scams from many popular messaging apps. We are partnering to bring this to additional Android users later this year. We are also expanding Android developer verification to protect people against malicious apps outside Google Play, wherever apps are distributed.

Industry alignment for collective defense

Beyond product solutions, defeating fraud networks requires coordination across experts and industries. Earlier this year, we joined industry peers to sign the Industry Accord Against Online Scams and Fraud, taking a collective approach to sharing threat intelligence and coordinating defenses. Building on the Industry Accord, we recently helped establish the Japan Anti-Scam Alliance (JASA) to enable public and private institutions to deploy aligned defenses.

Google.org also recently helped launch the Global Anti-Scams Philanthropy Collaborative to coordinate cross-industry philanthropic action against scams globally.

Efforts to strengthen community resilience

To strengthen resilience at the community level, today Google.org announced $6 million in funding to The Asia Foundation and the Tech for Good Institute to help small businesses and individuals in APAC to stay safe online. The efforts will include training local communities on building scam resilience, incubating AI-powered defense prototypes, and equipping policymakers with insights to strengthen threat measures.

This builds on Google.org’s ongoing support for local organizations, like Bamboo Builders in Singapore and the Taiwan FactCheck Center, to deliver specialized, hyper-local training to citizens. And it expands on the ASEAN Foundation’s Scam Ready ASEAN initiative, which is bringing online scam prevention resources to millions in the region. We are also expanding Be Scam Ready, an educational scam-awareness game — and one of the Scam Ready ASEAN’s program resources — to Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Vietnam. Be Scam Ready simulates common scams to prepare citizens, and is already available in Singapore, Thailand, and Taiwan.

Helping communities stay ahead of organized fraud is central to our work, and we will continue to advocate for a collaborative, global approach.

entries.title: Expanding AI educator training to new countries
entries.summary: An illustration featuring a stylized globe in the center with network lines connecting points across the world to various colorful icon badges, including graduation caps, award ribbons, and stylized figures.
entries.content:
Teachers around the world strive to find better ways to overcome challenges and meet each students' unique needs, and many have discovered how AI can become a powerful assistant in this effort.

That's why we created the Google AI Educator Series (GES): a no-cost, on-demand training designed to give educators practical AI skills they can use immediately and that fits into their busy schedule.

We first launched GES in the U.S earlier this year, and later expanded to India, Korea, Malaysia, Philippines, and the U.K & Ireland. In the coming months, we’re bringing GES to Brazil, Mexico, Spain, Australia, and sub-Saharan Africa.

A look at GES from teachers around the world

Here is a look at how educators around the world are turning their training into practical applications that save time, make lessons more engaging, and support student learning:

  • India: Teachers are using Gemini and Gemini Notebook to turn complex topics into comic strips, podcasts & infographics – making learning more accessible and engaging. Following September sessions that trained 80,000 educators, we’re bringing GES to all Indian educators with self-paced online modules. Aligned with National Education Policy 2020, the training is available in English & six local languages — Hindi, Marathi, Telugu, Assamese, Odia, Punjabi — with more coming next year.
  • Philippines: Educators are using Gemini to simulate complex market scenarios in economics classes and more, all to free up time for direct student guidance. To support this progress, we’ve partnered with the Philippine Department of Education, Commission on Higher Education, and Technical Skills Development Authority to bring AI training to over one million educators across the country. Building on this momentum, the Philippine Department of Education recently issued an official memorandum endorsing GES to all teaching and non-teaching staff nationwide.
  • Malaysia: Following the official launch of GES at BETT Asia, Malaysian teachers report saving three to five hours of prep time on curricula, assessments, and visual aids per topic, allowing them to focus on interactive, student-centered learning. As a next step, we are launching "train-the-trainer" bootcamps alongside local partners to expand GES training to private school educators, pre-service teachers, and university faculty nationwide.
  • United Kingdom: In the U.K., teachers are using tools like Gemini Notebook to develop learners’ creative writing skills and create engaging lesson plans and visuals. Through the launch of GES, all 650,000 teachers can receive digital literacy training by joining virtual or in-person events around the UK and Ireland. We are also hosting “train the trainer” workshops in the Google London office in November.
  • Korea: In partnership with Seoul National University of Education (SNUE), GES in Korea is aligned with the 2022 Revised Curriculum and the Ministry of Education's Teacher AI/Digital Education Competency Framework. Teachers are using Gemini and Gemini Notebook to design inquiry-based lessons and assessments while streamlining administrative tasks like parent communications and data analysis.

New November sessions

To ensure GES lessons are truly helpful, we update and create new content monthly in response to feedback from educators. Our November modules go live on November 4th in the U.S. focused on helping educators save time where they tell us they need it most.

Here's what's coming:

  • Build interactive assessments: Learn how to use Gemini to build practice tests and interactive web assessments — like exit tickets with instant feedback and hints for incorrect answers — to help students prepare for assessments like state exams..
  • Guide students through game-based learning: Guide students through interactive, game-based learning experiences that demonstrate the importance of data accuracy, model performance, and human oversight.
  • Strengthen academic assignments: Use Gemini to learn how to spot questions that can lead to taking shortcuts, helping faculty strengthen assignments and encourage deeper student critical thinking.

Earn your badge today and join a growing global community of educators.

entries.title: New research shows how Guided Learning supports students
entries.summary: Four students huddled in a circle, all looking at a laptop together
entries.content:
We’re sharing two new studies that show how Guided Learning supports students and teachers in real-world settings. Alongside these findings, today we’re starting to roll out Guided Learning in Google Classroom, giving teachers even more control over how and when this tool is used in their classrooms.

Guided Learning is designed to help students work through complex concepts step by step, prioritizing deep understanding over providing direct answers.

Boosting statistics scores

To see how Guided Learning impacts real performance, we conducted a randomized controlled trial (RCT) with more than 300 students at the University of Tokyo. We wanted to test whether Guided Learning provided extra value beyond standard study tools. All students were given half a day to independently study a statistics lesson using standard online resources. Half of the group was also given access to Guided Learning in the Gemini app.

Instead of looking for quick answers, students used Guided Learning to dig deeper. They frequently asked for practice quizzes, step-by-step help, and custom visual aids. When we compared pre- and post-test scores, the difference was clear. Students using only standard web tools improved their scores by 5.3 percentage points. But students with access to Guided Learning improved by 8.1 percentage points, representing 1.5x higher learning gains in just a single study session. While that number might seem modest — these gains were achieved in just half a day of study, pointing to growing evidence that when technology guides students rather than shortcutting the process, it can lead to more learning.

Giving teachers more insight and control

Bringing Guided Learning into Google Classroom requires a specialized approach that is purpose-built for the classroom, keeps teachers in control, and grounds the experience in relevant lesson materials.

To test this experience, we partnered with Ark and ran a four-week pilot across three UK secondary schools, allowing teachers to use Guided Learning in Google Classroom across four different subjects. Feedback from post-pilot surveys and interviews was encouraging: teachers found Guided Learning handled initial student questions effectively during independent work, so they had more time to offer targeted, one-on-one help. Meanwhile, the majority of surveyed students said they felt comfortable asking Gemini for help when stuck, and over half said it helped them solve problems on their own.

We also received important feedback on areas of improvement. Some teachers wanted clearer visibility into how their students were engaging with the course materials so they could better tailor future lessons. Others voiced a desire to keep their students focused on specific assignments during class time and reduce distractions. We took this feedback back to the team and made direct improvements — including adding insights for educators to show how their students interacted with Guided Learning, and improving the ability for teachers to anchor conversations on uploaded curriculum.

Shaped by real educator and student feedback in the classroom, today we're rolling out teacher-led Guided Learning globally in Google Classroom. This feature will help teachers assign their students a Guided Learning experience that will coach students step-by-step on their course materials and track student progress with actionable insights.

By grounding our tools in learning science, working alongside educators, and conducting research in real classroom settings, we're eager to continue innovating on tools that support active learning and a deeper understanding.
